artworks.title: Thisbe
artworks.description: Waterhouse's Thisbe listens at the crack in the wall — Pre-Raphaelite stillness for Ovid's Babylonian maiden who loved through a chink her fathers could not close.

artworks.title: Thisbe
artworks.description: Burne-Jones' Birmingham panel isolates Thisbe at the wall — part of his Pyramus and Thisbe cycle, the maiden framed as patient listener before the mulberry tragedy.

artworks.title: Thisbe (Sarjeant Gallery)
artworks.description: Another Burne-Jones Thisbe in the Sarjeant Gallery — the same Ovidian heroine as solitary figure, cloak and wall, waiting for a voice that will not save her.

artworks.title: Thisbe and Pyramus (House of Dionysos mosaic)
artworks.description: Floor mosaic from the House of Dionysos: Thisbe and Pyramus with the lion and mulberry already in the scene — Ovid's lovers as Roman domestic pavement myth.

popCulture.title: Metamorphoses
popCulture.creator: Ovid
popCulture.description: Book IV — the wall, the lioness, the sword, and the mulberry stained forever: Thisbe's defining telling.

popCulture.title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
popCulture.creator: William Shakespeare
popCulture.description: Flute as Thisbe — Shakespeare's mechanicals turn the Babylonian maiden into the funniest tragic heroine on stage.

popCulture.title: The Legend of Good Women
popCulture.creator: Geoffrey Chaucer
popCulture.description: Chaucer's Thisbe among the good women — medieval English reception of Ovid's wall-split romance.

popCulture.title: Pyramus and Thisbe
popCulture.description: The maiden who fled a lioness and died on her lover's sword — Ovid's template for tragic misunderstanding.
